title: India Is Negotiating to Sell Its Fastest Missile to the UAE. The Iran War Made It Possible.
excerpt: Talks to export BrahMos and the Akashteer air-defence system mark India's biggest defence pitch to the Gulf — and a direct counter to Pakistan's deepening ties with Saudi Arabia.
body:
The missile India wants to sell the United Arab Emirates can travel nearly three times the speed of sound, skim the sea at barely ten metres above the waterline, and hit a target 290 kilometres away before most air-defence systems register it as a threat. It is called BrahMos, and until very recently, only two countries had it: India and the Philippines.

Now, four Indian sources have told Reuters that New Delhi is in early but fast-moving discussions to sell BrahMos — along with the Akashteer automated air-defence command system — to Abu Dhabi. If the talks succeed, the deal would be India's most consequential defence export ever, and a signal that the post-Iran-war Gulf is reshaping its security architecture far more rapidly than anyone expected.

## Why the UAE Is Shopping

The war changed the calculus. When Iran launched strikes across the Gulf earlier this year, the UAE absorbed significant damage — and realised that its existing American systems, the THAAD and Patriot interceptors, were not enough on their own. Abu Dhabi has since gone on an arms-buying spree: a $35-billion memorandum of understanding with South Korea, accelerated procurement talks with European manufacturers, and now India.

"A diversified supplier base gives the UAE more strategic autonomy, and closer ties with India have the added benefit of not antagonising the U.S., as the countries remain allies," Pearl Pandya, South Asia senior analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data group, told Reuters.


![Abu Dhabi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Abu_dhabi_skylines_2014.jpg/3840px-Abu_dhabi_skylines_2014.jpg)



> **""Both the BrahMos missile and the Akashteer system would potentially serve the UAE's needs," he said."**



What the UAE wants from India is specific. BrahMos would give it a supersonic cruise missile launchable from land, sea and air platforms — a capability gap that the American ATACMS ballistic missile, with its similar 300-kilometre range, does not fully cover. Akashteer, meanwhile, is designed to knit together sensor data from multiple platforms into a single air-defence picture, improving response times against drones and cruise missiles — precisely the threats the Iran war demonstrated.

## The Russia Factor

There is a complication. BrahMos is jointly developed with Russia, and any export requires Moscow's sign-off. But Indian officials say this is unlikely to be a hurdle. Russia and the UAE maintain close diplomatic and energy ties; Moscow has no strategic reason to block the sale and every financial incentive to approve it.

The broader context matters more. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the United States supplied 54 per cent of all arms imported by the Middle East between 2021 and 2025, followed by Italy at 12 per cent and France at 11 per cent. India, which has historically been a net importer of weapons, barely registers on the list. A BrahMos sale to the UAE would change that — and give India a foothold in the world's most lucrative arms market.

## The Pakistan Dimension


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


Indian government sources told Reuters that the BrahMos discussions must also be understood against the recent defence pact between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Riyadh and Islamabad have deepened military cooperation over the past year, a development that New Delhi views with discomfort.

By arming Abu Dhabi, India would effectively be backing the UAE in a quiet rivalry with Saudi Arabia for Gulf leadership — and countering Pakistan's growing influence in the region by offering a competing security partnership.

Siemon Wezeman, a senior researcher at SIPRI, noted that while India has a track record of export discussions that do not always bear fruit, the current talks have more substance than past overtures. "Both the BrahMos missile and the Akashteer system would potentially serve the UAE's needs," he said.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

The UAE is home to 3.4 million Indians — the largest concentration of the diaspora anywhere in the world. A deeper defence relationship between New Delhi and Abu Dhabi reinforces the broader strategic partnership that underpins their security, their legal protections, and the bilateral agreements that govern everything from labour rights to consular access.

It also positions India as something more than a source of workers and remittances in the Gulf. For the first time, India would be a security provider to one of the region's wealthiest nations — a shift that recalibrates the power dynamic in a relationship the diaspora has long navigated from the weaker side.

*Sources: Reuters (exclusive), Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Armed Conflict Location & Event Data*
